chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
title: Whether Black musicians could read music
summary: McRae objects to the idea that Black musicians could not read, citing Armstrong, Jabbo Smith and Jenkins Orphanage graduates.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Like I told you before, when John Hammond say 'Come down to audition', I say, 'Well (inaudible) that idea.'
It was a thing when they was trying to get black musicians on the staff. And they probably said I don't know if they can read.
I say, 'What do you mean you can't read?
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
During this time, you were playing with all the top musicians in the coun-- all these bands -- black bands."
Like Fletcher Handerson, Duke Ellington. All your arrangers were writing for them. All these are top musicians.
These men studied and some of them are still studying.
Sure. All these musicians, the top musicians. They try to put out, say, "I don't know if black musicians can read."
Louie Armstrong -- they come out of homes. When they was -- Jabbo and all them guys come out of (inaudible) homes.
All of them guys come out of Jenkins Orphan Home. Top musicians. Play. You know, the best.
I mean, not no -- the best. I mean, they could read anything you put in front of them.
